title: Row Holding the Most Ones
statement:
You get a grid grid of 0s and 1s. The rows are not sorted. Find the row that contains the most 1s.

Return [row, count]: the row's index and how many 1s it holds. If several rows tie, return the one with the smallest index.

examples.why: Rows 1 and 2 both hold two 1s. The earlier row wins the tie.
Every row ties at zero, so row 0 is the answer.
Row 1 has three 1s. The rows are unsorted, so you have to count, not search for the first 1.

hints: Each row needs its own count; there is no shortcut when rows are unsorted.
Keep the best row and its count as you go.
Replace the best only when a row's count is strictly greater. That keeps the earliest row on ties.

explain.intuition:
Every cell can change a row's count, so every cell must be read: O(rows · cols) is the floor. Count each row's 1s, and keep the best so far.

The tie rule is handled by the comparison itself. Scanning rows top to bottom and replacing the best only on a strictly larger count means a later row that only ties never takes over. Start with [0, count of row 0], or with a best count of -1, so a grid of all zeros still returns row 0.
steps: For each row index r, count its 1s (the sum of the row).
If that count is greater than bestCount, store r and the count.
pitfalls: Using >= when comparing, which returns the last tied row instead of the first.
Starting bestCount at 0 with bestRow unset, then returning an invalid row for an all-zero grid.
Binary searching for the first 1 in each row. That only works when rows are sorted, and here they are not.

solutions.title: Count every row
solutions.idea: Sum each row and keep the first row with the strictly highest sum.

followups: Every row is sorted, all 0s before 1s. Can you beat O(rows · cols)?
Return all rows that tie for the maximum, in index order.
